per_quote.text: While previous research has identified the unique impact of both political orientation and political climate on vaccination attitudes, there has been little research on the interaction between personal political orientation and local political climate.
The present research examines political climate as a potential moderator of the association between political orientation and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.

our findings indicate that political climate, as represented through regional 2020 presidential election votes, has a stronger association with vaccine and booster hesitancy for individuals who are higher on political conservatism as compared to those who are politically liberal.

By looking at political orientation and region climate, we identify a novel and important finding, specifically that conservative individuals are more likely to received booster doses in liberal regions.
This was an online self-reported study in which a nonprobability convenience sample was recruited from the United States between March 8 and April 19, 2023.
We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023.

Both items were rated on a 11-point sliding scale from strongly liberal (0) to strongly conservative (10). These two items were averaged to form a political conservatism scale.
Vaccine hesitancy (i.e., negative attitudes toward vaccination) was measured using the seven items from the Attitudes towards Adult Vaccination Scale [24]
Booster hesitancy was assessed using items from a 2022 survey on COVID-19 booster hesitancy [25].
The present research presents a novel analysis of the dataset from this project, focusing on political orientation and political climate, rather than marginalization.

Multiple linear regression models were built to assess the association between political conservatism and conservative regional climate with vaccine hesitancy, controlling for age, gender, education, income, race, and perceived vaccine access.

Political conservatism and conservative regional climate were both associated with higher levels of COVID-19 vaccine and booster hesitancy and lower rates of self-reported vaccination and boosting, when controlling for age, education, income, and race.
As political conservatism increases vaccine hesitancy also increases, but this increase is even greater for individuals who live in a more conservative regional climate.

There was a similar pattern for booster hesitancy, with more politically conservative individuals in a conservative regional climate having higher booster hesitancy than conservative individuals in a liberal regional climate.

Our analysis reveals that politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries, with this effect particularly pronounced in the United States.

the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied.
Most existing research on adolescent networks derives from racially heterogeneous school settings, where substance use is often linked to friendship formation and popularity.

It remains unclear whether these patterns hold in settings where the student population is predominantly AI and where cultural norms surrounding kinship, community, and identity may differently orient relational processes.
This paper takes an initial step toward understanding these dynamics by investigating the role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties within AI‑majority schools.
Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.
